name: Razorpay
interview_style: Structured but fast-paced. Razorpay interviewers value clarity of thought and directness. They dislike long-winded answers. Expect deep dives into past work — they want specifics, not generalizations. Technical roles will have system design rounds.
what_they_look_for: Concrete examples of ownership — situations where you went beyond your role
Specific metrics and outcomes, not just actions taken
Genuine curiosity about fintech and payments
Ability to handle ambiguity without losing focus
Culture of shipping — they want doers, not planners
red_flags_for_them: Vague answers like 'we built a system' — they want 'I designed the schema and shipped it in 3 weeks'
Blaming external factors for failures without taking accountability
No curiosity about Razorpay's product or competitors
Risk aversion and over-emphasis on process
Inability to quantify your own impact
hr_round_focus: Why Razorpay specifically — they screen hard for genuine interest
How you handle failure — they want honesty and learnings
Team collaboration stories — how you dealt with conflict
Long-term career vision and how Razorpay fits
What you read, follow, and stay curious about
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a time you owned a project from ideation to launch. What was the hardest part?
Describe a situation where you had to push back on a senior stakeholder. How did you do it?
What's a product decision you've seen Razorpay make that you'd have done differently?
Tell me about a time you failed. What did you learn and how did you change?
Why fintech? Why payments? Why now?
founders_round_focus: Expect questions about the business model, growth levers, and competitive moat of Razorpay. They want people who think like owners, not employees.
recent_news_to_know: Razorpay's expansion into banking stack, RazorpayX, and their NBFC license are key talking points.

name: Swiggy
culture_values: Think big, start small, move fast
interview_style: Swiggy interviews are case-driven. Expect real business problems from Swiggy's operations or product. They value structured problem-solving and the ability to drive toward clarity from an ambiguous starting point. Behavioral interviews follow STAR format strictly.
what_they_look_for: Ability to break down complex operational or product problems
User empathy — especially for delivery executives and restaurant partners, not just consumers
Data fluency — can you move from intuition to insight with data?
Collaboration across functions without letting hierarchy slow you down
Track record of moving fast and shipping meaningful work
red_flags_for_them: Answers that ignore the operational complexity of food delivery
Over-indexing on consumer experience while ignoring supply-side (DE, restaurant)
No familiarity with Swiggy's product evolution or business model
Inability to size a problem or define success metrics
Excessive caution and analysis paralysis
hr_round_focus: Why Swiggy and why this specific role
Collaboration and conflict resolution stories
How you handle failure and recover
Examples of customer empathy in practice
Long-term ambitions and how Swiggy fits
sample_hr_questions: Swiggy operates at the intersection of logistics, tech, and food. What excites you most about that?
Tell me about a time you had to align multiple teams with different priorities. How did you get to a decision?
Describe a time you took a bold bet that didn't work out. What happened?
How do you stay close to users or customers in your current role?
What's one thing Swiggy does really well and one thing you'd improve?
founders_round_focus: Expect scenario questions: 'What would you do if delivery times increased 20% in Bengaluru this month?' They want structured thinkers who can operate across ambiguity.
recent_news_to_know: Swiggy's IPO, Instamart expansion, and the quick-commerce war with Blinkit are essential context.

name: Zepto
interview_style: Zepto interviews are intense, fast, and direct. They're built by 19-year-olds who dropped out of Stanford — expect a young, scrappy culture. Interviewers want to know if you'll take ownership immediately and if you can operate at startup speed. They don't appreciate over-prepared corporate answers.
what_they_look_for: Extreme ownership — stories where you went far beyond your job description
Speed of execution — how quickly can you move from idea to shipped?
Hustle — willingness to do whatever it takes, including things below your pay grade
Business impact — every project should have a number attached
No ego — flat hierarchy, willingness to take out trash if needed
red_flags_for_them: Process-heavy thinking ('we'd need to run this through several committees')
Inability to move without complete information
Focus on title or role boundaries
No metrics or numbers associated with your past work
Not using Zepto or not knowing its product deeply
hr_round_focus: Why startups, specifically Zepto
Evidence of hustle and going above and beyond
How you handle extreme ambiguity and fast change
Team fit — energy, attitude, drive
What you want to learn and build in next 2 years
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about the most ownership you've ever taken in a role — what was the situation and what did you do?
Describe a time you worked extremely fast under pressure. What was the result?
We move fast and sometimes break things. Tell me about a mistake you made when moving fast.
Why quick commerce? Why do you believe this is a long-term business?
What would you do in your first 30 days here?
founders_round_focus: Expect scenario questions about dark store economics, delivery time optimization, and grocery catalog strategy. Founders are very hands-on and technically sharp.
recent_news_to_know: Zepto's Series E fundraise, Zepto Cafe launch, and their dark store count expansion are key talking points.

name: Google
culture_values: Focus on the user and all else will follow
It's best to do one thing really, really well
You can be serious without a suit
interview_style: Google uses a structured, competency-based approach. All interviewers use a unified scorecard. Expect 4-6 rounds for senior roles. Heavy emphasis on Googleyness (cultural fit), Leadership (initiative, influence), Problem-solving, and Role-specific skills. Technical roles always include system design and coding.
what_they_look_for: Googleyness: intellectual humility, collaboration, thriving in ambiguity
Demonstrated impact at scale — your work reaching millions
Structured, first-principles problem solving
Leadership that doesn't depend on authority (influencing without hierarchy)
Continuous learning mindset and intellectual curiosity
red_flags_for_them: Arrogance or unwillingness to acknowledge weaknesses
Can't work in large, matrixed organizations
Only individual contributor mindset with no leadership evidence
Inability to deal with ambiguity or changing requirements
Not enough intellectual depth — surface-level answers
hr_round_focus: Googleyness — will you thrive in Google's unique culture?
Leadership examples from all levels of seniority
How you handle failure and what you've learned
Collaboration across large, complex organizations
Why Google vs. other big tech companies
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a time you influenced an outcome without having direct authority.
Describe a situation where you had to work with someone whose work style was very different from yours.
Tell me about a project that failed. What was your role and what did you take away from it?
Give me an example of when you had to learn something completely new in a short time frame.
Why Google specifically, and why this role at this point in your career?
founders_round_focus: Google's 'founders round' equivalent is usually the hiring committee or VP review. Expect questions about long-term vision, impact at Google-scale, and how you'd approach big bets.
recent_news_to_know: Gemini AI, Google Cloud growth vs. AWS, antitrust scrutiny on Search, and Workspace AI integration are essential.

name: Amazon
culture_values: Ownership — act like an owner, never say 'that's not my job'
Dive deep — stay connected to details
interview_style: Amazon is famous for the Leadership Principles (LPs). Every single behavioral question maps to one or more LPs. Prepare 2-3 STAR stories per LP. Interviewers will probe hard if your story is vague — they want specifics: who, what, when, numbers. Technical roles have system design + coding. PMs have product case + LP rounds.
what_they_look_for: Customer obsession — you start every decision from the customer
Ownership — you go beyond your role and drive things to completion
Dive deep — you know the details of your work, not just the surface
Frugality — you've done more with less, you don't throw resources at problems
Bias for action — you make decisions with incomplete information and move fast
red_flags_for_them: Vague STAR stories — 'we did X' without your specific role
No metric or outcome in your examples
Inability to 'disagree and commit' — you either agree too easily or hold grudges
Entitlement or arrogance — Amazon is anti-hierarchy
No customer empathy — every answer must trace back to the customer
hr_round_focus: Bar Raiser round — a senior Amazonian who checks LP compliance across all 16 principles
Deep STAR story probing for every LP
Specifically: Customer Obsession, Ownership, Invent & Simplify, Dive Deep
Why Amazon and why this team
Long-term career vision
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a time you sacrificed short-term gains for a better long-term outcome for the customer.
Describe a time you took on something significantly outside your responsibilities.
Tell me about a time you invented a process or tool that simplified work for others.
Give me an example of when you dug into data that wasn't readily available to find an answer.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision and what you did about it.
founders_round_focus: Amazon doesn't have a traditional founders round, but the Bar Raiser serves a similar function. They focus on LP depth and whether you'll raise the bar for Amazon's culture.
recent_news_to_know: AWS AI/Bedrock expansion, Amazon India strategy, generative AI infrastructure investments, and Project Kuiper (satellite internet) are key.

name: Flipkart
culture_values: Build from the heart — serve Indian customers
Be bold and take big bets
interview_style: Flipkart interviews are similar to Amazon's in structure — expect behavioral STAR questions — but with a distinctly Indian market context. Case interviews for PM and strategy roles. Technical interviews include system design with a focus on scale (they operate at very high transaction volumes).
what_they_look_for: Deep understanding of Indian consumers and Bharat market
Ability to think at Flipkart-scale (400M users, millions of sellers)
Entrepreneurial mindset — Flipkart was India's first e-commerce startup
Willingness to build for challenges unique to India: low bandwidth, price sensitivity, COD
Data fluency and ability to interpret large-scale behavioral data
red_flags_for_them: Western-centric product thinking without adaptation for India
No understanding of Bharat users (Tier 2-4 cities, vernacular needs)
Inability to think at scale
Not aware of Flipkart's competitive position vs. Amazon India
Arrogance about your current company vs. Flipkart
hr_round_focus: Why Flipkart over Amazon India
Your relationship with and understanding of Indian consumers
Stories of building or adapting products for diverse user segments
How you collaborate in large, matrixed orgs
Long-term goals and how Flipkart enables them
sample_hr_questions: What do you know about Bharat users that most product people in Bengaluru don't?
Tell me about a time you made a decision that was right for the customer but hard internally.
Describe a high-stakes project where you had to align 5+ teams. How did you do it?
What's one thing Amazon India does better than Flipkart, and how would you fix it?
Tell me about a product or feature that failed. What went wrong and what did you learn?
founders_round_focus: Flipkart's senior rounds focus on market strategy, Bharat expansion, and long-term competitive moat. They want people who've thought deeply about Indian e-commerce.
recent_news_to_know: Flipkart's IPO plans, Walmart ownership, Flipkart Quick (quick commerce push), and their logistics subsidiary eKart are key talking points.

name: CRED
interview_style: CRED interviews are unusually conversational and creative for a fintech company. They expect strong opinions and the willingness to defend them. Design sensibility is assessed even for non-design roles. They will probe your taste — what products do you admire and why? Vague answers fail immediately.
what_they_look_for: Taste and design sensibility — you notice when products are beautiful vs. merely functional
Strong opinions, loosely held — you have a point of view and can defend it
Ownership — you don't just do your job, you shape your role
Trust-building — every CRED product is built on trust with creditworthy members
Deep thinking — CRED dislikes shallow, trend-following thinkers
red_flags_for_them: No opinion about product design or no design taste
Generic answers about why you want to work in fintech
Not using CRED or not knowing their product deeply
Thinking of premium users as a niche — CRED sees 12M creditworthy Indians as a massive market
Short-term thinking — CRED bets on 5-10 year trust relationships
hr_round_focus: Cultural alignment — trust, transparency, craft
Your product taste and opinions about design
Why CRED vs. any other fintech
How you build trust with users in your work
Long-term vision and ambition
sample_hr_questions: What's a product you think is genuinely beautiful? Why — be specific about what they got right.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager and what you did about it.
What do you think CRED's core business model is? Do you believe in it long-term?
Describe the last time you went significantly beyond what was asked of you.
What would you fix about CRED's product in your first 90 days?
founders_round_focus: Kunal Shah (CEO) rounds focus on mental models, contrarian thinking, and first-principles reasoning about consumer behavior and trust economics. He has a famous framework called 'Delta 4' — know it.
recent_news_to_know: CRED's UPI push, CRED Mint (P2P lending), and their expansion into car financing through CRED Garage are recent developments.

name: Groww
culture_values: Long-term user benefit over short-term revenue
interview_style: Groww interviews are straightforward and merit-based. Expect strong emphasis on domain knowledge (investing, financial products) and ability to make complex things simple. They value intellectual honesty and will call out BS quickly. Technical rounds are rigorous.
what_they_look_for: Passion for financial inclusion — making investing simple for first-time investors
Data fluency — every decision at Groww starts with a number
Simplicity mindset — can you make a complex financial product understandable?
Trust-building — financial products require an especially high trust bar
Domain knowledge — mutual funds, stocks, ETFs, and their regulatory landscape
red_flags_for_them: No interest in personal finance or investing
Over-engineered solutions to simple problems
Regulatory naivety — financial products have hard constraints
No empathy for first-time investors
Inability to quantify past impact
hr_round_focus: Why financial services and why Groww
Your own relationship with investing — do you invest? What do you own?
How you build user trust in high-stakes domains
Collaboration and alignment stories
Long-term vision and how Groww fits
sample_hr_questions: Do you personally invest? What do you own and why did you make those choices?
Tell me about a time you simplified something complex for a non-expert audience.
What's one thing Groww does that builds trust with first-time investors, and one thing that could erode it?
Describe a situation where data told you one thing but your gut said another. What did you do?
How would you explain a SIP to someone who has never invested before?
founders_round_focus: Groww founders (Lalit, Harsh, Neeraj, Ishan) focus on mission alignment, financial inclusion vision, and long-term user trust. They want true believers.
recent_news_to_know: Groww's expansion into US stocks, FD products, and their IPO preparations are key. Also know Groww's valuation trajectory.

name: Meesho
interview_style: Meesho interviews are centered around the Bharat user — interviews will probe whether you genuinely understand Tier 2-4 India. Expect detailed behavioral interviews with a focus on empathy and impact. They want people who can do more with less — frugality is core to their DNA.
what_they_look_for: Deep empathy for Tier 2-4 India users — resellers, small sellers, value-seeking buyers
Frugality — can you solve problems without spending money?
Impact at massive scale — Meesho reaches users that other platforms ignore
Diversity appreciation — Meesho's team is intentionally diverse
Long-term commitment — Meesho plays a 10-year game
red_flags_for_them: Bengaluru/Mumbai bubble thinking — no understanding of Bharat
Resource-heavy solutions ('we'd need 3 engineers and a data scientist')
No empathy for low-income, first-time online shoppers
Not understanding Meesho's supplier-reseller-buyer three-sided marketplace
Short-term P&L thinking without considering long-term relationship economics
hr_round_focus: Your connection to Bharat users and communities
Why Meesho's mission resonates with you personally
Frugality stories — doing more with less
Collaboration and inclusion examples
Long-term ambition and patience
sample_hr_questions: Describe a product experience you've had as a customer in a Tier 2-3 city context. What was broken?
Tell me about a time you achieved significant results with very limited resources.
What do you think is the single biggest barrier to internet commerce adoption in small-town India?
Describe a time you worked with a team that was very different from your background.
Why Meesho over Flipkart or Amazon India for your career?
founders_round_focus: Vidit Aatrey (CEO) focuses on mission alignment, Bharat user empathy, and long-term strategic bets. He will probe whether you've actually spent time understanding non-metro India.
recent_news_to_know: Meesho's path to profitability, their social commerce model evolution, and expansion into D2C for small brands are key.

name: PhonePe
culture_values: Owned by users, powered by trust
Build for 10 years, ship in 10 days
interview_style: PhonePe interviews are rigorous, data-driven, and move fast. Expect technical depth even for PM roles. They value people who've operated at scale (PhonePe processes 5B+ transactions/year) and have a zero-tolerance for downtime. Culture is intensely performance-driven.
what_they_look_for: Scale mindset — your instincts should be calibrated for hundreds of millions of users
Reliability obsession — payments require five-nines uptime thinking
Data fluency — PhonePe makes almost no decisions without data
Speed — they compete with Paytm and Google Pay in real time
Financial inclusion mission — serving users who never had bank accounts before
red_flags_for_them: Naive about payment regulations (RBI, NPCI, UPI framework)
No appreciation for uptime and reliability requirements
No data or numbers in past work
No understanding of UPI as an ecosystem, not just a feature
Western-centric product thinking
hr_round_focus: Why payments, why PhonePe
Examples of operating at high scale with reliability requirements
How you think about trust in financial products
Collaboration stories across large orgs
Long-term vision for digital India
sample_hr_questions: What do you think has been PhonePe's single biggest advantage over Google Pay and Paytm?
Tell me about a time you were responsible for something that broke in production. How did you handle it?
How would you explain UPI to a 60-year-old vegetable vendor in rural Rajasthan?
Describe a data-driven decision you made that overrode your gut instinct. How did it turn out?
What's one new product PhonePe should build and why?
founders_round_focus: Sameer Nigam (CEO) focuses on 'why payments, why India, why now' — mission alignment and long-term strategic thinking. He wants people who've thought deeply about the digital infrastructure layer of India.
recent_news_to_know: PhonePe's ONDC integration, international expansion plans, and their IPO timeline are key. Also know their dominance in UPI market share.

name: Atlassian
interview_style: Atlassian is famous for STAR-based behavioral interviews called 'strength-based' interviews. They do NOT do trick questions or brainteasers. Expect questions about collaboration, intellectual honesty, and openness. Technical roles have coding and system design. Culture is remote-first and very collaborative.
what_they_look_for: Openness and intellectual honesty — no posturing, just truth
Genuine teamwork — Atlassian is deeply collaborative, no lone wolves
Mission connection — they believe in unleashing the potential of every team
Balance — they actually care about burnout and sustainable pace
Initiative and self-direction — remote-first requires strong autonomy
red_flags_for_them: Competitive or 'win at all costs' attitude
Inability to be honest about failures or weaknesses
Micromanagement tendencies
No appreciation for work-life balance
Need for constant manager input to make decisions
hr_round_focus: Atlassian values alignment — specifically the 5 values
Collaboration and team-first stories
How you give and receive feedback
Remote work effectiveness
Why Atlassian and why B2B SaaS
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a time you had to give difficult feedback to a colleague. How did you approach it?
Describe a situation where the team made a decision you disagreed with. How did you handle it?
How do you maintain strong team relationships in a remote-first environment?
Tell me about a time you put the customer's interest ahead of a business metric.
What does 'open company, no bullshit' mean to you in practice?
founders_round_focus: Atlassian co-founders Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar built on values of openness and balance. Senior interviews probe whether you'll add to or subtract from that culture.
recent_news_to_know: Atlassian's acquisition of Loom, team anywhere (remote-first) strategy, and AI features in Jira and Confluence are key.

name: Microsoft
culture_values: Make more possible — empower every person and organization
interview_style: Microsoft interviews use behavioral questions mapped to their cultural attributes: Growth Mindset, Collaboration, Customer Obsession, and Diversity & Inclusion. Satya Nadella's influence (growth mindset) is pervasive. Technical rounds are thorough. They value intellectual humility and continuous learning.
what_they_look_for: Growth mindset — learn from failure, stay curious, embrace change
Collaboration across extremely large, complex organizations
Customer empathy, especially for enterprise and developer customers
Diversity perspective — they mean it, not just as HR exercise
Ability to operate with patience and long-term thinking (Microsoft moves slower than startups)
red_flags_for_them: Fixed mindset — 'I'm already good at X, I don't need to improve'
Inability to operate in a large, matrixed organization
Short-term thinking — Microsoft plays 10-year games
No curiosity or continuous learning in your work history
Ego or arrogance
hr_round_focus: Growth mindset examples — specifically learning from failure
Collaboration in large, diverse teams
Customer empathy and customer impact
Inclusion stories
Why Microsoft and why now (Azure AI moment)
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a time you had to fundamentally change your approach or way of thinking about a problem.
Describe a situation where you collaborated effectively with people from very different backgrounds or perspectives.
Tell me about a time you failed to meet a customer's expectations. What happened and what did you learn?
How do you create an inclusive environment in your team?
What does the growth mindset mean to you, and give me a specific example of you practicing it.
founders_round_focus: Microsoft's equivalent is the as-ap (as appropriate) loop which includes a senior principal or VP. They focus on strategic thinking, cross-organization impact, and culture contribution.
recent_news_to_know: Microsoft's Copilot AI integration across Office, OpenAI partnership and investment, Azure growth, and GitHub Copilot are essential.

name: Juspay
culture_values: Reliability and trust — payments never fail
interview_style: Juspay is an engineering-first company built by IIT/BITS engineers who care deeply about systems reliability. Interviews are technical and deep. They value people who have read source code, built production systems, and care about correctness. They're not a growth-hack company — they're an infrastructure company.
what_they_look_for: Deep technical craftsmanship — you care about how things are built, not just that they work
Reliability mindset — understanding that payments require 99.99% uptime
Payments domain knowledge — UPI, card networks, PCI-DSS
Long-term relationship builder — Juspay's moat is trusted, long-term enterprise relationships
Open source ethos — Juspay has open-sourced core payment infrastructure
red_flags_for_them: Move fast and break things mentality — Juspay cannot afford breaks in production
No systems thinking — everything at Juspay involves distributed systems
Short-term deal mentality
No familiarity with payments ecosystem
Dismissiveness toward Haskell or functional programming (Juspay uses Haskell in production)
hr_round_focus: Why infrastructure/platform companies appeal to you
Your relationship with technical depth and craftsmanship
How you build trust with large enterprise clients
Long-term career commitment
Open source philosophy and community
sample_hr_questions: Tell me about a system you built that you're genuinely proud of — technically, not just business-impact-wise.
Describe a time you had to build something where correctness was more important than speed.
What do you think is the most underrated aspect of payments infrastructure that most PMs/engineers ignore?
Tell me about a long-term relationship you've built with a client or partner. What made it last?
Have you used any open-source projects in production? Have you contributed back?
founders_round_focus: Vimal Kumar (CEO) focuses on technical depth, payments ecosystem understanding, and long-term commitment. He specifically tests for people who think in systems and reliability.
recent_news_to_know: Juspay's Hyperswitch open-source payment orchestration layer and their processing of 40B+ in annual volume are key.

name: Paytm
culture_values: Vijay Shekhar Sharma's vision — financial services for the masses
interview_style: Paytm interviews are intense and sales/execution-focused. Expect a fast-paced environment reflected in the interview style. They value people who are willing to roll up sleeves and do whatever it takes. There's less of the structured behavioral framework and more of a direct conversation style.
what_they_look_for: Hustle and intensity — Paytm's culture is demanding
Scale appetite — they think in hundreds of millions of users
Sales mindset even in non-sales roles — everyone at Paytm is expected to drive growth
Comfort with complexity — Paytm has many business lines
Loyalty and long-term commitment
red_flags_for_them: Work-life balance as a primary concern in early interviews
No understanding of Paytm's complexity (payments + lending + insurance + commerce + ticketing)
Slow decision-making tendencies
Perceived lack of intensity
No understanding of regulatory challenges Paytm has faced
hr_round_focus: Why Paytm specifically — they're aware of their reputation challenges
Comfort with fast-paced, demanding environments
Stories of outworking challenges
Understanding of digital payments ecosystem in India
Long-term commitment to financial services
sample_hr_questions: Paytm has faced challenges in the last few years. What do you think about the company's path forward?
Tell me about the most demanding work environment you've been in. How did you handle it?
What do you think about the RBI's recent actions on Paytm Payments Bank? How would you address them?
Describe a time you drove revenue or growth directly.
Why financial services for mass-market India over premium fintech?
founders_round_focus: Vijay Shekhar Sharma is known for vision conversations about financial inclusion and building for the masses. He wants believers in the digital India story.
recent_news_to_know: RBI action on Paytm Payments Bank (2024), Paytm's stock decline, restructuring, and path to profitability are essential. This is a sensitive topic — be informed and measured.

name: Zomato
culture_values: Customer obsession (customer = diner, restaurant, delivery partner)
Think 10x — big bets over incremental moves
interview_style: Zomato interviews are direct and fast. Deepinder Goyal's transparency culture permeates the interviews — they want honest people who won't sugarcoat. Expect hard questions about Zomato's business model, profitability path, and the three-sided marketplace. Cultural fit is assessed through honesty and directness.
what_they_look_for: Three-sided marketplace thinking: diner, restaurant partner, delivery partner
Radical transparency and honesty — including about your own failures
High-velocity execution — Zomato moves extremely fast
Sustainability mindset — Zomato has made real environmental commitments
Big bet thinking — Zomato entered quick commerce (Blinkit) against all odds
red_flags_for_them: One-sided customer thinking — forgetting restaurant and DE experience
Inability to be honest about failures
No familiarity with Zomato's business model evolution
Incremental thinking when 10x is expected
No appreciation for the gig economy and DE welfare
hr_round_focus: Why food tech and why Zomato
Your view on the three-sided marketplace and unit economics
Stories of radical honesty and transparency
Big bet examples — a time you made an ambitious call
Deepinder Goyal's transparency principle — how you embody it
sample_hr_questions: What do you think is the single hardest problem Zomato faces in the next 3 years?
Tell me about a time you were radically honest with someone — a manager, a colleague, or a report.
Zomato acquired Blinkit at a time when everyone called it a bad deal. What's your view?
Describe a time you made a big bet that seemed risky at the time. What happened?
How would you improve the delivery partner experience at Zomato?
founders_round_focus: Deepinder Goyal is known for candid, unfiltered conversations. He asks about what you'd do differently at Zomato, and he means it — he wants your actual opinion.
recent_news_to_know: Zomato's Blinkit acquisition and integration, path to profitability, and Hyperpure B2B expansion are essential.
